summary: RFC 4090 defines local repair techniques for rerouting RSVP-TE traffic over pre-established backup tunnels, including the facility method. This document defines a version of facility protection that does not depend on refresh intervals.

eli5.summary: If a road closes, traffic switches onto a prepared detour. This improves how routers handle that detour without constant re-checking.

subtitle: Extra teardown rules so RSVP-TE fast reroute can clean up stale state without relying on short refresh timers.

tldr.problem: RSVP-TE Fast Reroute with facility backup (RFC 4090) implicitly depends on short refresh timeouts to clean up stale LSP state, which clashes with long refresh intervals used for scaling.
tldr.mechanism: Routers set up a Node-ID Hello session between the repairing router and the merge point, and use a Conditional PathTear and a Remote PathTear to delete or keep state explicitly instead of waiting for timeouts.
tldr.outcome: Facility backup becomes refresh-interval independent and compatible with the RI-RSVP capability of RFC 8370. It updates RFC 4090 and is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 9705 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2025. It updates RFC 4090, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Refresh Timeouts Are a Problem
sections.content:
RSVP-TE keeps the state of each Label Switched Path (LSP) alive with periodic refresh messages. If refreshes stop, the state is deleted automatically. This is a scaling burden as the number of LSPs grows, so RFC 2961 lets a router stretch the refresh interval well beyond the default 30 seconds of RFC 2205.

The Fast Reroute (FRR) extensions in RFC 4090 still implicitly rely on short refresh timeouts to clean up stale state when bypass tunnels are used. This document adds explicit teardown procedures so that facility backup no longer depends on the refresh interval. It assumes reliable delivery of RSVP messages as specified in RFC 2961.
sections.eli5: Routers normally keep saying 'I am still here' every so often. If you make them say it less often, they also notice problems more slowly, so they need a faster way to announce changes.

sections.title: The Problem on a Failed Link
sections.content:
The RFC uses a topology with a path A, B, C, D and two detours (through E and F). Many LSPs run from A to D through B and C, with node protection configured. If the B-C link fails, B repairs locally onto its bypass LSP B, F, D. B then creates a backup state and signals it to D. Meanwhile C stops receiving refreshes and times out the protected LSP state.

RFC 4090 leaves several problems unspecified:

  • If C times out and tears down before D hears about the backup LSP, D receives a PathTear first and deletes the LSP state.
  • If C keeps state until timeout, a long refresh interval means a large amount of stale state on C. If C deletes it and tears down toward D, D loses the LSP.
  • If the head-end A tears the LSP down after the repair but before B signals the backup, B may delete its state without telling D, leaving stale state on D.
  • If B fails to repair locally, B deletes state without informing D, with the same result.
sections.eli5: When a bridge collapses, one town might throw away the map to the next town before the detour is announced, or keep an old map forever. Both are bad, so the towns need clear rules.

sections.title: The Signaling Handshake Between PLR and Merge Point
sections.content:
The Point of Local Repair (PLR) is the router that redirects traffic onto a bypass LSP. The Merge Point (MP) is the router where the bypass rejoins the protected path. An LP-MP protects against a link failure and an NP-MP protects against a node failure.

To let the MP know it is an MP, the PLR does the following:

  • It picks the router ID of the NNHOP or NHOP node from the Node-ID sub-object in the Record Route Object (RRO) as the bypass destination.
  • It adds its own router ID in a Node-ID sub-object in later Path messages.
  • It starts a Node-ID-based Hello session with the MP, with TTL set to 255 because the two routers may not be neighbors. The MP must set the I-bit in the CAPABILITY object of its Hello messages.
  • It attaches a B-SFRR-Ready Extended ASSOCIATION object (from RFC 8796) to the Path message, with the Association Source set to its Node-ID address.

A node that finds a matching B-SFRR-Ready object naming itself as bypass destination, and has a working Node-ID adjacency with the advertised PLR, must consider itself an MP. It then keeps a "remote" path state, which differs from the normal state only in the RSVP_HOP object. That state lets the PLR later tear down the LSP remotely.
sections.eli5: The router that starts the detour phones the router where the detour ends, so that router knows it is the meeting point and can wait for the detour traffic.

sections.title: What Each Router Does When a Failure Happens
sections.content:
Failures are detected through Node-ID Hello sessions. What a router does depends on its role.

  • Not an MP: if its previous-hop (PHOP) link or node fails, it MUST send a Conditional PathTear and delete its path and reservation state.
  • LP-MP: after a PHOP link failure it MUST keep the state until the Node-ID adjacency with the PLR goes down, or it receives a normal or Remote PathTear or a ResvTear. If it detects PHOP node failure, it sends a normal PathTear and deletes the state.
  • NP-MP: after a PHOP link or node failure it MUST keep the state until the remote adjacency with the PPHOP PLR goes down, or it receives a PathTear or ResvTear. It also keeps state if it receives a Conditional PathTear from its PHOP.
  • Both LP-MP and NP-MP: it keeps the state until the relevant adjacencies are gone or a tear arrives.

In the example, when the A-B link fails, B is not an MP and deletes its state. C is the NP-MP for A, so it keeps state, removes the B-SFRR-Ready object for B from its Path message and triggers a Path to D. D then learns it is no longer the NP-MP for B and deletes the matching remote state.
sections.eli5: Each router has a rule for its job. A router that is not part of a detour cleans up. A router that is waiting for a detour holds on until it is told the detour is done or cancelled.

sections.title: Conditional PathTear and the CONDITIONS Object
sections.content:
A Conditional PathTear is a PathTear that carries a new optional CONDITIONS object. A router that is not an MP sends it when its PHOP link or Node-ID adjacency fails, provided the ingress requested node protection and no PathTear was received from upstream.

A receiving router that is not an NP-MP treats it as a normal PathTear: it deletes its state, removes the object and sends a normal PathTear downstream. An NP-MP MUST NOT delete the LSP state. If the PHOP had earlier sent a B-SFRR-Ready object, the NP-MP removes it and triggers a Path downstream. A sender that has not advertised support is treated as sending a normal PathTear.

The object has Class 135, C-type 1 and a 32-bit flags field. Bit 31 is the Merge-point condition (M) bit: when set, the PathTear is processed according to the receiver's role, and when clear it is processed as normal. Bits 0 to 30 are reserved. The Class-Num follows the pattern 10bbbbbb so an implementation that does not know the object ignores it and handles the message as a normal PathTear.
sections.eli5: It is a note stapled to a cancellation: 'cancel this unless you are the meeting point.' Routers that cannot read the note just cancel.

sections.title: Remote PathTear and Preemption
sections.content:
A Remote PathTear is sent from a PLR straight to the MP, with TTL 255, to delete LSP state when the PLR has not yet signaled the backup path. The PLR sends one in these cases:

  • The ingress tears the LSP down during local repair, before backup signaling completes. The MP deletes the path and reservation states.
  • Local repair fails. The MP deletes its state and propagates the PathTear downstream to the egress. For link protection, the tear goes to the LP-MP's Node-ID address.
  • A change in the Resv RRO shows the former NP-MP is no longer on the path. The PLR sends a Remote PathTear to that former NP-MP.

If an LSP is preempted on an LP-MP or NP-MP after its PHOP link failed but before backup signaling, the node sends a normal PathTear and deletes its state. In the RFC's example, D then rejects B's later backup Path message with a PathErr, and B deletes its reservation and sends a ResvTear to A.
sections.eli5: If the detour plan is cancelled, the starting router can call the meeting point directly and say 'forget it', instead of passing the message along the whole road.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility and Deployment
sections.content:
A node supporting RFC 4090 facility backup MUST NOT set the RI-RSVP flag (I-bit) from RFC 8370 unless it supports all the extensions in this document. A node that supports them MUST set the flag in its Hello CAPABILITY object; otherwise neighbors treat it as unsupporting.

When a downstream node (the NHOP, or the NNHOP when node protection is requested) lacks support, the node MUST reduce the refresh period in the Path TIME_VALUES object to the default short interval and MUST NOT send Remote or Conditional PathTears. In the example the default short interval is 30 seconds. The upstream rules are symmetrical, using Resv messages, and a node that reduces refresh time MUST NOT run the MP procedures.

The extensions can be enabled per direction, so a region of upgraded routers gets the benefit even if the rest of the network has not been upgraded. The RFC also shows what goes wrong if a node sets the I-bit without support: stale state can linger for the long refresh timeout, or a Conditional PathTear can be misread as a normal one and tear down the LSP.
sections.eli5: If a neighbor does not know the new rules, a router goes back to the old, slower way of checking in, so nothing breaks.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The security considerations of the original RSVP specifications (RFC 2205, RFC 3209 and RFC 5920) still apply. When RSVP cryptographic authentication is used, stronger algorithms such as HMAC-SHA256, HMAC-SHA384 or HMAC-SHA512 SHOULD be used where possible.

Because Node-ID Hello sessions may now run between non-neighbors, implementations SHOULD allow a per-neighbor or global Node-ID authentication key, and administrators SHOULD use it to authenticate Hello messages received with a TTL greater than 1. Implementations SHOULD also let operators limit the number of Node-ID Hello sessions.

IANA added Class Number 135 (CONDITIONS) with C-Type 1 to the RSVP Parameters registries, and created a "CONDITIONS Object Flags" subregistry in which bit 31 is the Merge-point flag. New values need IETF Review.
sections.eli5: Because routers now talk to routers farther away, they should check who they are talking to and not accept too many such conversations.

fields.name: Class
fields.desc: Class number of the CONDITIONS object.

fields.name: Flags (Reserved)
fields.desc: Bits 0-30 are reserved: set to zero on transmission and ignored on receipt.

fields.desc: Merge-point condition bit: when set, process the PathTear according to the receiver's role.
